description: Hi, I am Faustino. I'm currently studying Environmental Engineering. In the past, I also studied Computer Science, earning a Bachelor's degree in that field. So, now I'm basically looking to mix my two fields of study and to get the best of both worlds.
summary: MODIS and VIIRS both detect active fires, but VIIRS (375 m) reports about 3.3 times more hot spots than MODIS (1 km) over Argentina, so a count series that moves from one sensor to the other jumps with no change in fire. With Terra and Aqua being retired, that break is about to hit every long fire record. fire-calendar harmonizes NASA FIRMS hot spots from 2000 to today into two comparable scales, MODIS-equivalent and VIIRS-equivalent, using a scale factor per 2.5° block, month and day/night, with 80 % conformal uncertainty bands. The factor was validated leave-one-year-out (block-year WAPE about 10 %) and beat both a quantile-matching baseline and a LightGBM model, so the simple method is the one published. Continuity after MODIS and after S-NPP (ended 2026-11-02) goes through NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. The web app shows a year × month calendar, anomalies against the climatology, an ENSO row (association, not cause) and CSV downloads for every Argentine province and department, starting from Córdoba. It is retrospective, not an alert system.
details:
What it does. A Python pipeline downloads NASA FIRMS per-country files (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS S-NPP, NOAA-20) and, for recent months, data from the FIRMS area API. It filters the detections (type 0, MODIS confidence ≥ 30, VIIRS nominal or high), grids them at 0.1° and converts each sensor to the other’s scale with a frozen, checksummed calibration. Every modeled number carries its source, period and an uncertainty band. Years before VIIRS existed (2000–2011) are labelled “estimated”. A web app shows the result as a year × month calendar, anomalies against the climatology, an ENSO phase row and CSV downloads for every Argentine province and department. It opens on Córdoba.

How it was validated. Leave-one-year-out and rolling-origin tests over 2012–2025, and a simulated MODIS switch-off (cut-offs 2021–2024: block-year WAPE 12.3 %). It also includes drift checks on Terra and Aqua and a pre-registered comparison against baselines.

Machine learning, tested and reported. LightGBM models (Poisson/Tweedie) were trained in both directions on rows of one 0.1° cell, one month and day or night. They started from the scale factor as an offset, so they could only add corrections to it. Features: hot-spot count, fire radiative power (FRP) and FRP per detection, count over the 3×3 neighbourhood, the day/night share, the count of the other half of the day, the block total and the month. Latitude/longitude and the Terra/Aqua share were tried only as ablations. The most used features were FRP per detection (47 % of gain) toward MODIS and the 3×3 neighbourhood count (67 %) toward VIIRS. Adding MODIS MCD64A1 burned area as a variable changed nothing (+0.08 points). The rule for publishing ML was fixed before the run. VIIRS→MODIS came close (block-month WAPE 15.9 % vs 17.2 %) but failed on bias (−2.5 % vs +0.9 %), so the published series uses the simple factor.

What comes next.

Validate the factor on the first full fire season after MODIS and S-NPP (2026). The frozen uncertainty bands have only been checked on January–April 2026.

An experimental outlook: the probability that next month has more hot spots than the area’s median, up to 6 months ahead. It would use ENSO (ONI and its forecast), drought (SPEI), fire weather (FWI) and the previous month’s anomaly. Logistic regression and LightGBM would be scored against climatology, persistence and ENSO-analog years. Predictions would be frozen in a registry and shown as “Experimental, not an alert”. If they don’t beat climatology, the app says so.

Atmospheric rivers and fire in the Andes and Patagonia: whether a very wet season relieves fire right away or grows fuel for the next dry one.

Land cover as a variable, and the official Córdoba boundary.

Benefits and impact. Researchers, fire brigades and provincial agencies can read trends and anomalies across the sensor change. That way a satellite switch isn’t mistaken for a change in fire activity, and the series keeps going after MODIS is retired.

Tools. Python 3.12 (uv, pandas, LightGBM), FastAPI, TypeScript + React + MapLibre GL, Vitest and Playwright, GitHub Actions, and Cloudflare Pages, which serves static JSON per province and department.

What we considered. Honesty over polish: unverified items are marked as such, ENSO is shown as an association only, and the app is explicitly retrospective, not an alert system. The interface is in Spanish, with a full English version.
dataRefs: ASA FIRMS active fire data (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS 375 m)
